THIS FILE IS FOR ADDRESSING ISSUES WITH THE JSON DATA FROM THE "SPECIES IDENTIFICATION" WORKFLOWS.

The JSON data is not structured the same way for each set of zooniverse output, so we need a way to map all of the possibilities and handle the data effectively.

## Overview

Output from classifications on the [Zooniverse](https://zooniverse.com) come encoded in *JSON format*. While most of the columns are straightforward to interpret, two critical columns are not. The first is the **annotation column**. Within it are the species identification and the answers to all of the questions for each event. Likewise, the **subject_data** column contains all of the information from the manifest, such as the forest type, photo batch, camera number, and forest name. It would be good to be able to pull all of this information. We especially need it if we plan to remove e.g. images taken on malfunctioning cameras or otherwise suspect images. It looks like we can parse the subject data across all of the workflows and workflow versions, but cannot parse the annotations column across all workflows and workflow versions.

Assuming you are working with the complicated zooniverse data (through August 2026), you will need the following steps:

1\. Parse the `subject_data` column from the entire zooniverse dataset. To do so you will use the new (Nov 2026) `flatten_subjects` function.

2.  Subset the data by workflow and workflow version. Those files are obtained from the `1.Parse_workflows.Rmd` file in the previous step.

<!-- -->

2.  Parse the annotations column for each workflow. The annotations column is the column in the zooniverse classification file that includes all of the answers to the questions in the zooniverse workflow, including what the species is and what the animals are doing.

3.  

4.  Join the annotation & subject_data together into a data frame for further data analysis.

5.  Write the output to a folder called "Flattened" in the PostZooniverse Output folder.

While this is all well and good, the code below also has some data checking built in, for work being done in November, 2026 working with 4 versions of the workflow Zooniverse 16695, Species identification.

### Turn on packages and bring in the data and r scripts

### Step 2. Obtain metadata about the file {#step-2}

Let's gather some information about this data file and create a data frame in which to gather it. Based on what you did using `1.Load_data_from_googledrive.qmd` you may have dataframes in a list. That's what we'll assume here in Method C below.

#### Method A assumes you have a list with separate data frames as elements. {#method-a}

We'd like to collect some information about each of the dataframes we're going to be evaluating as metadata. Let's store the metadata as a dataframe with one row of information per dataframe. We'll use a loop so that we can iterate over the elements in `select_list` to extract metadata.We created `select_list` with the code in `1.Load_data_from_googledrive.qmd`.

```{r}
#create empty dataframe to store results

File_metadata <- data.frame(list_element_name = character(),
                            wkflow_id = numeric(),
                            wkflow_name = character(),
                            wkflow_version = numeric(),
                            num_unflattened_rows = numeric(),
                            num_unique_classifications = numeric(),
                            num_unique_subjects = numeric())

for(i in 1:length(select_list)){

#extract first element from select_list as temp_df
temp_df  <- map_dfr(select_list [i ], rbind)

#create empty df to hold metadata
temp_meta  <- data.frame(list_element_name = character(length = i),
                         wkflow_id = numeric(length = i),
                         wkflow_name = character(length = i),
                         wkflow_version = numeric(length = i),
                         num_unflattened_rows = numeric(length = i),
                         num_unique_classifications = numeric(length = i),
                         num_unique_subjects = numeric(length = i))

temp_meta [i, 1 ]  <- names(select_list [i ])
temp_meta [i, 2 ]  <-unique(temp_df $workflow_id)
temp_meta [i, 3 ]  <-unique(temp_df $workflow_name)
temp_meta [i, 4 ]  <-unique(temp_df $workflow_version)
temp_meta [i, 5 ]  <-length(temp_df $classification_id)
temp_meta [i, 6 ]  <- length(unique(temp_df $classification_id))
temp_meta [i, 7 ]  <- length(unique(temp_df $subject_ids))

#now assign to File_metadata DF
File_metadata  <- File_metadata |> add_row(temp_meta [i, ])
}

```

#### Save the metadata

### Step 3. Parse the JSON data

Our JSON data, especially in the subjects column (which has info about camera number, sd card number, image names, etc. and comes in part from the zooniverse manifest) is really messy because not all of the rows have JSON data in the same structure. The result is that it is difficult to parse into columns. Further, some data are encoded in different ways for different subjects. For example, in some, the JSON for camera number is CamNum and for others it is cam_num. We'd like to be able to get this all condensed into the same columns and not add a bunch of extraneous, redundant columns that then have to be reconciled.

I'm using ChatGPT for some code suggestions, though the code below is all my own.

#### Subset to one dataframe

I'm going to work through each data frame so that I can try to understand better why some rows lack camera information after the join. It may have to do with slightly different workflow versions not parsing the same way.

Let's get a list of elements present in our list

```{r}
dataframes <- names(select_list)
```

Now we can easily grab one of the 4 dataframes. Let's start with workflow version 11.8.

```{r}
df <- map_dfr(select_list [1 ], rbind)
#use if extracting dataframe from list
```

This is a very large file - let's reduce to a random subset of 250 rows

```{r}
random_subset <- sample_n(df, 250)
```

Three column contain JSON data: - metadata - annotations - subject_data

We need information from the annotations and subject_data columns

#### Explore JSON data

```{r}
flat_file <-flatten_annotations(df)

#this is slow; could we write faster code? A problem for another day.
```

####Annotations JSON data The annotations column contains the data that identify the animal and that answer all of the zooniverse questions (did the deer have antler, etc.)

Now that we have the data loaded, we will first flatten the Annotations column by calling the `flatten_annotations` function. Then we extract subject information with the `flatten_subjects_wflow_32_13` function. We join and clean up the data and can then export it for later use.

The first section of code ("Method A") subsets each dataframe one at a time so that I can look for wonkiness before merging to one large data frame.

The code under "Method B" uses a loop to step through each dataframe in `select_list` and extract subject and annotation data from each and then adds data from each dataframe to a single, final dataframe that includes data from more than 1 workflow version.

#### Method A. Single dataframe and data checks

I'm going to work through each data frame so that I can try to understand better why some rows lack camera information after the join. It may have to do with slightly different workflow versions not parsing the same way.

Let's get a list of elements present in our list

```{r}
dataframes  <- names(select_list)
```

Now we can easily grab one of the 4 dataframes. Let's start with workflow version 11.8.

##### Collect summary information here

As I work through these 4 dataframes I'm going to collect some information about them here:

Let's create a dataframe to store information:

```{r}

workflow_summary_details  <- data.frame(

wkflow_version = numeric(length(dataframes)),

num_rows = numeric(length(dataframes)),

num_rows_flat_file = numeric(length(dataframes)),

num_subjects_not_in_flat = numeric(length(dataframes)),

num_unique_subjects = numeric(length(dataframes))

)

```

##### Workflow version 11.8

###### A. Parse the annotation data (Species ID and answers to questions)

Work with first dataframe

```{r}

df  <- map_dfr(select_list [1 ], rbind)

#use if extracting dataframe from list

#df  <- #point to your dataframe

flat_file <-flatten_annotations(df)

#this is slow; could we write faster code? A problem for another day.

```

Does the flattened file have fewer rows than the initial dataframe? If so, check.

Let's see which `subject_ids` in the main data frame are missing from the flattened file:

```{r}
not_in_flat  <- setdiff(df $classification_id, flat_file $classification_id)
```

Now let's take a look at those rows of data

```{r}

df[not_in_flat, ]|> View()

```

You can see that the difference are rows of data for which a classification was not completed, entirely composed of "NAs".

So, flat_file has all of the data for which a classification was actually made.

Are there any rows or columns of data in flat_file that are entirely NA?

```{r}

#check rows

flat_file |>
  filter(if_all(everything(), is.na)) |>
  View()

#check columns

flat_file |>
  select(where( ~all(is.na(.)))) |>
  View()
```

###### B. Parse the subjects column

Now we can parse the data.

Which function you use to flatten the subjects data depends on what version of the workflow you are using. Here's a guide.

The general `flatten_subjects` function was designed to parse a variety of different workflow versions, but results in many columns that need to then be matched. Let's try to refine a bit.

```{r}

#view json data from random sample of rows of dataframe

View_subject_data(sample_n(df, 10), 10)

```

Let's get 100 random rows of data from df to play with

```{r}

rand_subset_df <- df |> sample_n(100)

```

Let's try parsing subjects with general function from these rows:

```{r}
rand_subjects  <- flatten_subjects(rand_subset_df)
```

All applies for workflow 16695 - Species Identification

\|Workflow version \|Function to use \|

\|---------------- \|--------------- \|

\|11.8 \| `flatten_subjects_wkflow11.8` \|

If you are working with a recent version of the species identification workflow, use the `flatten_subjects_wflow_32_13.R` function.

```{r}

subjects <-flatten_subjects_wkflow11.8(df)

```

Now let's look at the rows of subjects for which no classification was made:

```{r}

subjects_not_classified  <- subjects [not_in_flat, ]

```

There are no subject IDS - we don't have any information in those rows, so we don't need them. Remove them so that subjects and flat_file are the same length.

If you are using data from an older workflow, there may be some wonky issues when you flatten subjects -- use the basic `flatten_subjects` function if that is the case.

I've updated flatten_subjects so that it reports a lot of columns, parsing all of the subject columns regardless of the format of the manifest that was uploaded to the zooniverse. So now we can sort by project and isolate data from different manifests that use the same workflow.

Notice that if flat_file may have fewer rows than subjects it is because for some subset of the data (equal in number to the difference in length b/w the subjects data and the flat_file data) no identification was made, so the annotations column has no information.

##### C. Merge the annotations and subjects data

Now that we have flattened both the annotations and subject_data columns, we would like to generate one large data frame with all of the data to export and analyze (using different R scripts!). To do so, we need to join the two data frames. Joining will \* *only work* \* if you have a column, named identically in both data frames, on which the join will work.

The join itself is pretty easy:

```{r}

Flattened_11_8  <-left_join(flat_file, subjects, by='classification_id')

 # Now move subject_ids column to left most position

Flattened_11_8 <-Flattened_11_8 %>% relocate(subject_ids)

#and see how many don't have image information

Flattened_11_8  |>
  filter(is.na(Img1)) |>
  View()

#find classifications for which no image info is present

NA_cam_info <- Flattened_11_8 |>
  filter(is.na(Img1)) |>
  select(classification_id)

#now look at those rows in df and look at some json data to understand why

#look at subjects

subjects |>
  filter(classification_id %in% NA_cam_info) |>
  View()

#look at flat_file

flat_file |>
  filter(classification_id %in% NA_cam_info) |>
  View()

#and move the Camera_SD card combination toward the left as well.

#next may not work depending on workflow version.

Flattened  <- Flattened  |>
  relocate(CamSD, .after = classification_id)

```

##### D. Fix dates and delete empty columns

Fix Dates One thing we should do for determining consensus picks is to correct the dates associated with the date-time of the first image in each subject set.

```{r}

Flattened <- Flattened |>
  mutate(newDTO_img1 = parse_date_time(DTO_Img1, c("mdy_HM", "ymd_HMS", "ymd")))

Flattened <- Flattened |>
  relocate(newDTO_img1, .after = DTO_Img1)

```

Delete empty columns Next, get rid of any empty columns in the dataset:

```{r}

empty_cols  <- sapply(Flattened, function(x)all(is.na(x))) #identify the columns that only contain NA

dump  <- which(empty_cols == TRUE)

Flattened <- Flattened  |>
  select(!dump)

```
